Fix a force model of the force branch [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: a
nondegenerate open time window $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, an open configuration
domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ for $N\ge1$ particle labels, with the
collision set removed when the model's force law is singular there
([[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a)), fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), and a force map
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$$
with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz hypotheses of clause
(iii) of that postulate. Fix one inertial frame of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]) and read all times and positions
below in this frame; dimensions and units are those of [[def-cm01-units]].

**Protocol.** An **operational observable model** of this force model in the
frame consists of the following data.

1. **Parameters.** A nonempty set $\Theta$, the **model parameters**, with a
   family $(F_{\theta})_{\theta\in\Theta}$ of force maps on
   $I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$, each satisfying the standing
   hypotheses of the force branch, so that $\bigl(I_{0},Q,(m_{i}),F_{\theta}\bigr)$
   is a force model of that branch for every $\theta\in\Theta$.
2. **Preparations.** A nonempty set $Z$, the **apparatus and preparation
   settings**, and a map $\zeta:Z\to I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$,
   written $\zeta(z)=\bigl(t_{0}(z),x_{0}(z),v_{0}(z)\bigr)$, assigning to
   each setting an initial datum of the model.
3. **Observation times.** A finite strictly increasing family
   $t_{1}<\dots<t_{k}$ in $I_{0}$ with $k\ge1$, the **observation times**.
4. **Definedness.** For every $(\theta,z)\in\Theta\times Z$ the model with
   force map $F_{\theta}$ and initial datum $\zeta(z)$ has a unique maximal
   motion $x_{\theta,z}:J_{\theta,z}\to Q$, with $J_{\theta,z}\subseteq
   I_{0}$ an open interval containing $t_{0}(z)$
   ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]], [[pthm-cm02-ivp]]), and the protocol requires
   $[t_{1},t_{k}]\subseteq J_{\theta,z}$. Its **state** at $t_{j}$ is
   $$s_{\theta,z}(t_{j}):=\bigl(x_{\theta,z}(t_{j}),\,w_{\theta,z}(t_{j})\bigr) \in Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N},$$
   where $w_{\theta,z}:=x_{\theta,z}'$ is the coordinate velocity.
5. **Readout.** An integer $d\ge1$ and a map
   $$R:\Theta\times Z\times\bigl(\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N}\bigr)^{k} \longrightarrow\mathbb R^{d},$$
   the **readout**, whose value at $(\theta,z)$ is the tuple of the $k$
   states of clause 4 in order; the **prediction map** is
   $$\Phi:\Theta\times Z\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{d},\qquad \Phi(\theta,z):=R\bigl(\theta,z,s_{\theta,z}(t_{1}),\dots, s_{\theta,z}(t_{k})\bigr).$$
   No regularity of $R$ in the parameters is assumed; continuity,
   differentiability or measurability in $\theta$ or in the states is an
   additional hypothesis, declared where it is used.
6. **Units.** For each $j\le d$ a dimension $[\Phi_{j}]$ from
   [[def-cm01-units]] is declared, and the coordinate $\Phi_{j}(\theta,z)$ is
   read in the corresponding unit.
7. **Error and observation.** A probability space $(\Omega,\mathfrak F,
   \mathbb P)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]), an open **error domain**
   $V\subseteq\mathbb R^{d}$ with $0\in V$, and a random element
   $\varepsilon:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{d}$ with $\varepsilon(\omega)\in V$ for
   every $\omega$ ([[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]). The
   **observation** at $(\theta,z)$ is the random element
   $$Y_{\theta,z}:=\Phi(\theta,z)+\varepsilon:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{d},$$
   the sum being read coefficientwise in the declared units, so that the
   coordinate $\varepsilon_{j}$ carries the dimension $[\Phi_{j}]$ for every
   $j$ (rule (b) of [[def-cm01-units]]).

### Well-definedness and conventions

**Well-definedness.** The prediction map is well defined: for each
$(\theta,z)$ the maximal motion is unique by [[pthm-cm02-ivp]], and clause 4
puts the observation times in its interval. For fixed $(\theta,z)$ the
observation is a random element in the sense of
[[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]: the map
$\tau(u):=\Phi(\theta,z)+u$ is a translate of $\mathbb R^{d}$, hence
continuous, its preimages of Borel sets are Borel, and
$Y_{\theta,z}^{-1}(B)=\varepsilon^{-1}\bigl(\tau^{-1}(B)\bigr)\in\mathfrak F$
by the measurability of $\varepsilon$. This repeats the argument of
[[def-cm-measurement-model]] for the additive-error observation model with
$h=\Phi$; the mathematical interface used below is exactly that definition.

**No hypothesis on the error is part of the definition.** Mean zero,
square-integrability, boundedness, a stated law, independence across
repetitions, stationarity and calibration are **not** part of the definition;
each must be stated at its point of use, with its exact quantifiers, exactly
as in [[def-cm-measurement-model]]. In particular a deterministic error, for
which $\varepsilon$ is a constant random element, is admitted; the definition
then records a modelled residual rather than a probabilistic error.

**Frame relativity of the protocol.** The observation times are times of the
declared frame, and the prediction map is read in that frame's coordinates;
a change of inertial frame changes the coordinate times and the readout of
the same physical protocol. The framework therefore always names the frame
in which a protocol is specified; no frame-independent reading of $\Phi$ or
$\varepsilon$ is asserted.

**Scope.** The definition constructs an interface, not a measurement. It does
not assert that any apparatus realizes the protocol, that any preparation can
be reproduced, that the declared error domain or law is correct, or that
$\Phi$ agrees with any physical system. A statement that a physical procedure
satisfies the protocol requires separate empirical evidence, and no such
evidence is part of this item.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is **totally differentiable at $a$** when there is a linear map $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) such that

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2}{\|h\|_2}=0,$$

where the quotient is considered for $h\ne0$ with $a+h\in U$. The map $L$, when it exists, is denoted $Df(a)$ and called the **total derivative**. Equivalently, $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r(h)$ with $\|r(h)\|_2/\|h\|_2\to0$.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have second partial derivatives. Its **Hessian** at $a\in U$ is the matrix $H_f(a)=(\partial_i\partial_j f(a))_{i,j<m}$ in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]], using the multi-index notation of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. A point $a$ is **critical** when its gradient $\nabla f(a)$ is zero, with the gradient convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $m,d\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $\mu\in U$, and let
$h:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be Borel measurable and totally differentiable at $\mu$
with total derivative $A:=Dh(\mu):\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^d$
([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]); for instance this
holds when $h$ is $C^1$ on $U$, since continuous maps have Borel preimages of
Borel sets ([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]). Let
$X:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be a random element with values in $U$,
square-integrable with mean vector $E[X]=\mu$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$
([[def-cm-covariance-matrix-of-a-random-vector]]), and define the
**linearization**
$$T:U\longrightarrow\mathbb R^d,\qquad T(x):=h(\mu)+A(x-\mu).$$
Then $T\circ X$ is a random element of $\mathbb R^d$, its mean vector is
$$E\bigl[T(X)\bigr]=h(\mu),$$
and its covariance matrix is
$$\operatorname{Cov}\bigl(T(X)\bigr)=A\Sigma A^{\mathsf T},$$
where $A$ is identified with its Jacobian matrix
$\bigl(\partial_jh_i(\mu)\bigr)_{i,j}$ and $A\Sigma A^{\mathsf T}$ is the
matrix product of [[thm-matrix-multiplication-laws]] in the matrix space of
[[def-matrix-space]].

Let $(\Omega,\mathfrak F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space
([[def-probability-measure]]), let $m\ge1$, and let
$X=(X_1,\dots,X_m):\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be a random element with target
$(\mathbb R^m,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m))$ that is **square-integrable**:
$$E\bigl[|X|^2\bigr]=\sum_{i=1}^{m}E\bigl[X_i^2\bigr]<+\infty ,$$
where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
Its **mean vector** is
$$\mu=E[X]:=\bigl(E[X_1],\dots,E[X_m]\bigr)\in\mathbb R^m ,$$
the coordinates being the expectations of
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Its **covariance matrix** is the
$m\times m$ real matrix of [[def-matrix-space]]
$$\Sigma=\operatorname{Cov}(X):=\bigl(\Sigma_{ij}\bigr)_{i,j=1}^{m},\qquad \Sigma_{ij}:=E\bigl[(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)\bigr]\in\mathbb R .$$
For a random vector $Y$ the entries $\Sigma_{ij}$ are also written
$\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$, and $\Sigma_{ii}=\operatorname{Var}(X_i)$.

### Well-definedness and elementary properties

**Integrability of the entries.** Square-integrability gives
$E[X_i^2]<+\infty$ for each $i$. Since $X$ takes values in a probability
space, the elementary inequality
$$|X_i|\le \tfrac12\bigl(1+X_i^2\bigr)$$
and monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) show that each
$X_i$ is integrable, so $\mu_i=E[X_i]$ is a finite real number
([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]). Likewise
$$|X_i-\mu_i|\le |X_i|+|\mu_i|\le \tfrac12\bigl(1+X_i^2\bigr)+|\mu_i|,$$
so $X_i-\mu_i$ is square-integrable and integrable. Finally
$$|(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)|\le \tfrac12\bigl((X_i-\mu_i)^2+(X_j-\mu_j)^2\bigr),$$
and the right-hand side is integrable by additivity, monotonicity and
homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]],
[[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]); hence every
$\Sigma_{ij}$ is a finite real number.

**Symmetry.** For all $i,j$ the real numbers $(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)$ and
$(X_j-\mu_j)(X_i-\mu_i)$ are equal pointwise, so $\Sigma_{ij}=\Sigma_{ji}$;
thus $\Sigma^{\mathsf T}=\Sigma$.

**Positive semidefiniteness.** Let $z=(z_1,\dots,z_m)\in\mathbb R^m$. The
random variable $W:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_iX_i$ is a finite linear combination of
square-integrable random variables, hence square-integrable, and bilinearity
of covariance ([[lem-variance-and-covariance-identities-for-random-variables]])
gives
$$z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=\sum_{i,j=1}^{m}z_iz_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j) =\operatorname{Cov}(W,W)=\operatorname{Var}(W) =E\bigl[(W-E[W])^2\bigr]\ge0 ,$$
the inequality holding because $(W-E[W])^2\ge0$ pointwise and expectation is
monotone ([[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]). In
particular $z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=0$ exactly when $W$ is almost surely
constant, so $\Sigma$ is positive definite exactly when for every $z\neq0$
the random variable $\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_iX_i$ fails to be almost surely
constant.

No independence hypothesis is used anywhere in this definition; $\Sigma$
records the pairwise covariances of the coordinates.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex
([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]), let $h:U\to\mathbb R$ be of class
$C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and let $B\in[0,+\infty)$
satisfy
$$\bigl\lVert H_h(x)\bigr\rVert\le B\qquad\text{for every }x\in U,$$
where $H_h(x)$ is the Hessian of $h$ at $x$
([[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]) and $\lVert\cdot\rVert$ is the
operator norm on the finite-dimensional inner-product space of real
$m\times m$ matrices ([[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]).
Then for all $\mu,y\in U$,
$$\bigl\lvert h(y)-h(\mu)-\nabla h(\mu)\cdot(y-\mu)\bigr\rvert \le\frac{B}{2}\,\lvert y-\mu\rvert^2 ,$$
where $\nabla h(\mu)\cdot(y-\mu)$ is the Euclidean pairing
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, let $h:U\to\mathbb R$
be of class $C^2$, and let $B\in[0,+\infty)$ satisfy
$\lVert H_h(x)\rVert\le B$ for every $x\in U$
([[lem-cm-uniform-second-order-remainder-bound]]). Let
$X:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be a random element with $X(\omega)\in U$ for every
$\omega$, with $E[X]=\mu\in U$ and $E\lvert X-\mu\rvert^2<+\infty$, and put
$$R:=h(X)-h(\mu)-\nabla h(\mu)\cdot(X-\mu).$$
Then $R$ is integrable and
$$\lvert E[R]\rvert\le E\lvert R\rvert \le\frac{B}{2}\,E\lvert X-\mu\rvert^2 .$$
If moreover $E\lvert X-\mu\rvert^4<+\infty$, then $R^2$ is integrable and
$$E\bigl[R^2\bigr]\le\frac{B^2}{4}\,E\lvert X-\mu\rvert^4 .$$

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

derivations.claim: On $U$ the function $l\mapsto 4\pi^{2}l$ is a polynomial and $T\mapsto T^{-2}$ has derivative $-2T^{-3}$ by [L2], so the product rule gives $\partial h/\partial l=4\pi^{2}T^{-2}$ and $\partial h/\partial T=4\pi^{2}l\cdot(-2T^{-3})=-8\pi^{2}lT^{-3}$, which the identity $h=4\pi^{2}lT^{-2}$ turns into $h/l$ and $-2h/T$; hence $Dh(\mu)=\bigl(h(\mu)/l_{0},\,-2h(\mu)/T_{0}\bigr)$.

Differentiating the first derivatives with the same rules gives $\partial^{2}h/\partial l^{2}=0$, $\partial^{2}h/\partial l\partial T=-8\pi^{2}T^{-3}$ and $\partial^{2}h/\partial T^{2}=24\pi^{2}lT^{-4}$, the symmetric Hessian $H_{h}$ of clause 2 of the statement; for $(l,T)\in U_{B}$ one has $T>T_{0}-\rho_{T}>0$ and $l<l_{0}+\rho_{l}$, so the moduli of the two second derivatives are below $8\pi^{2}(T_{0}-\rho_{T})^{-3}$ and $24\pi^{2}(l_{0}+\rho_{l})(T_{0}-\rho_{T})^{-4}$; since the Euclidean operator norm of a real symmetric $2\times2$ matrix is at most its Frobenius norm, the square root of the sum of the squares of the entries, $\lVert H_{h}(x)\rVert\le B$ holds on $U_{B}$ with the displayed $B$.

The map $h$ is $C^{2}$ on the open convex $U$, hence totally differentiable at $\mu$ with $Dh(\mu)$ as in step 1.1, and $X$ takes values in $U_{B}\subseteq U$ with mean $\mu$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$, so [L3] identifies the covariance matrix of $T_{\mu}(X)$ as the $1\times1$ matrix $Dh(\mu)\Sigma Dh(\mu)^{\mathsf T}=\bigl(h(\mu)/l_{0}\bigr)^{2}\sigma_{l}^{2}-2\bigl(h(\mu)/l_{0}\bigr)\bigl(2h(\mu)/T_{0}\bigr)\sigma_{lT}+\bigl(2h(\mu)/T_{0}\bigr)^{2}\sigma_{T}^{2}$; substituting $h(\mu)=4\pi^{2}l_{0}/T_{0}^{2}$ gives the three terms of clause 3, and at $\sigma_{lT}=0$ the relation $Dh\Sigma Dh^{\mathsf T}=h(\mu)^{2}\bigl(\sigma_{l}^{2}/l_{0}^{2}+4\sigma_{T}^{2}/T_{0}^{2}\bigr)$ follows by factoring out $h(\mu)^{2}=16\pi^{4}l_{0}^{2}/T_{0}^{4}$.

Steps 1.1 and 2.1 exhibit $h$ as $C^{2}$ on the open convex box $U_{B}$ with $\lVert H_{h}\rVert\le B$ there, and $X$ takes values in $U_{B}$ with $E[X]=\mu$; [L4] with this $B$ gives the pointwise bound, the two mean bounds and the squared-moment bound of clause 4, the last under its stated fourth-moment hypothesis.

Let an inertial frame $(o,u,(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}))$ of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ be fixed, and let $\gamma:I\to A$ be the worldline of a
particle label described in this frame as in [[post-cm01-worldlines]]; thus
$\gamma$ is of class $C^{2}$, parametrized so that $t(\gamma(s))=s$ for all
$s\in I$, and

$$\gamma(s)=o+su+\sum_{j=1}^{3}\xi_{j}(s)\,e_{j}$$

for the unique coordinate functions $\xi_{j}:I\to\mathbb R$ of the point
$\gamma(s)$ in the adapted chart ([[def-cm-affine-time-space]],
[[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]]).

**(a) The coordinate curve.** The **coordinate curve** of $\gamma$ in the
frame is

$$x_{\gamma}:=\bigl(\xi_{1},\xi_{2},\xi_{3}\bigr):I\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3}.$$

It is of class $C^{2}$ by the regularity clause of [[post-cm01-worldlines]],
and it determines $\gamma$ by the display above, since the parameter condition
fixes the time coordinate. It has dimension $[\,\xi_{j}\,]=\ell$
([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(b) Coordinate velocity and acceleration.** The **derivative** of a
vector-valued map is taken componentwise: for the map $x_{\gamma}$ above, its
derivative at $s$ is

$$x_{\gamma}'(s):=\bigl(\xi_{1}'(s),\xi_{2}'(s),\xi_{3}'(s)\bigr),$$

where each $\xi_{j}'(s)=\lim_{h\to0}\bigl(\xi_{j}(s+h)-\xi_{j}(s)\bigr)/h$ is
the ordinary derivative of a real function. The **coordinate velocity** of the
label in the frame is

$$w(s):=x_{\gamma}'(s)\in\mathbb R^{3},$$

with components $w_{j}=\xi_{j}'$, and the **coordinate acceleration** is the
coordinate velocity of the velocity,

$$a(s):=w'(s)=x_{\gamma}''(s)\in\mathbb R^{3}.$$

Their dimensions are $[w_{j}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $[a_{j}]=\ell\tau^{-2}$, read
in metres per second and metres per second squared. The triple $w(s)$ is the
triple of numbers read in the frame's axes: it is a coordinate description,
not an element of spacetime.

**(c) Spatial velocity and acceleration vectors.** The frame's time direction
$u$ and spatial basis identify two elements of the spatial displacement space
$K$ attached to the motion:

$$\underline{v}(s):=\gamma'(s)-u=\sum_{j=1}^{3}w_{j}(s)\,e_{j}\in K,\qquad \underline{a}(s):=\gamma''(s)=\sum_{j=1}^{3}a_{j}(s)\,e_{j}\in K.$$

Here $\gamma'(s)-u$ indeed lies in $K=\ker\tau$, because $\tau(\gamma'(s))=\frac{d}{ds}\tau(\gamma(s))=1$ by linearity of $\tau$ and the parameter condition. The vectors $\underline{v}(s)$ and $\underline{a}(s)$ are the **spatial velocity vector** and **spatial acceleration vector** of the label in the frame; they are frame-dependent objects of $K$, and their coordinates in the frame's basis $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$ are the triples $w(s)$ and $a(s)$.

**(d) Speed.** The **speed** of the label in the frame at time $s$ is the
Euclidean norm $\|w(s)\|_{2}=\sqrt{\sum_{j}w_{j}(s)^{2}}$, of dimension
$\ell\tau^{-1}$; equivalently $\|\underline{v}(s)\|_{2}=\sqrt{g(\underline{v}(s),\underline{v}(s))}$,
the norm induced by the spatial metric, since the basis is $g$-orthonormal.

**(e) Transformation under a change of inertial frame (recorded).** Let a
second inertial frame be given, with coordinates $(t',x')$ and transformation
parameters $(b,a,v,R)$ as in [[post-cm01-frames]], and let
$\eta(t'):=x'(\gamma(t'-b))\in\mathbb R^{3}$ be the description of the motion
in the second frame. Then

$$\eta'(t')=R\,w(t'-b)+v,\qquad \eta''(t')=R\,a(t'-b),$$

that is, in the differentiated variables and abbreviated notation
$w'=Rw+v$ and $a'=Ra$. This law is clause 2 of the mathematical transformation
law of [[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]], recorded here
in the model's notation; the definition itself asserts neither law. The
model-level statement of the law, including the frame-independence of the
property $a\equiv0$, is proved as a theorem later on this page.

Let a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] be given: time window
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ nondegenerate and open, configuration domain
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ open ([[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a)),
fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), and a
force map $F$ with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz
hypotheses of clause (iii) of that postulate.

**(a) State domain and inverse-mass operator.** The **state domain** of the
model is

$$D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},$$

an open subset of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{6N}$; a point $(t,x,v)\in D$ is a
time together with the **state** $z=(x,v)$ of positions $x\in Q$ and coordinate
velocities $v\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ of the labels ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]],
[[def-cm01-units]]). The **inverse-mass operator** is the linear map

$$\mathsf M^{-1}:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathsf M^{-1}(u_{1},\dots,u_{N}):=\Bigl(\frac{u_{1}}{m_{1}},\dots,\frac{u_{N}}{m_{N}}\Bigr),$$

the inverse of the mass operator $\mathsf M$ of clause (d) of
[[def-cm01-configuration]].

**(b) Associated first-order system.** The **associated first-order field** of
the model is

$$\mathcal F:D\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathcal F(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)\Bigr),$$

and the **associated first-order system** is $z'=\mathcal F(t,z)$ on the open
domain $D$, in the sense of
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]; here
$z=(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{6N}$. The map $\mathcal F$ satisfies the
Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]: it is continuous on
$D$, and it is locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z$ locally uniformly
in time, because its first component $z\mapsto v$ is linear and its second is
the composition of the force map $F$ — which is locally Lipschitz in $(x,v)$
locally uniformly in time by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iii) —
with the linear map $\mathsf M^{-1}$.

**(c) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior, endpoints read with one-sided derivatives as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$ such that
$t\in I_{0}$ for every $t\in J$ and

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J).$$

Equivalently: the state curve $z=(x,\dot x):J\to D$ is a solution of the
associated first-order system on $J$. Indeed, if $x$ is a motion then
$z=(x,x')$ is $C^{1}$ with
$z'=(x',x'')=(x',\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,x'))=\mathcal F(t,z)$ and $z(t)\in D$;
conversely, if $z=(x,v)$ is a solution with $z(t)\in D$ for all $t$, then
$x'=v$ and $v'=\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)$, so $v$ is $C^{1}$, $x$ is $C^{2}$, and
multiplying the second equation by the masses returns the displayed
second-order equation. Motions of the labels of the model are exactly these
curves by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iv).

**(d) Initial data and maximal motion.** An **initial datum** of the model is
a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $t_{0}\in I_{0}$, $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; write $z_{0}:=(x_{0},v_{0})$. A **maximal
motion** with this datum is a motion $x:J_{\max}\to Q$ with $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $\dot x(t_{0})=v_{0}$ that has no extension to a motion of the model on a
strictly larger interval. By the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses verified in (b)
and the maximal-solution theorem
[[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]] (with
[[def-maximal-ode-solution]]): every initial datum has exactly one maximal
motion, its **maximal interval** $J_{\max}$ is an open interval containing
$t_{0}$ and contained in $I_{0}$, and every motion with the same datum is the
restriction of the maximal one. The restriction statement transfers from the
associated first-order system to motions through the equivalence in (c).

**(e) Newtonian flow.** The **Newtonian flow** of the model is the map

$$\Phi:\Omega\longrightarrow Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \Omega:=\bigl\{(t,t_{0},z_{0}):t_{0}\in I_{0},\ z_{0}\in Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\ t\in J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})\bigr\},$$

defined by $\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0}):=z(t)$, where $t\mapsto z(t)=(x(t),\dot x(t))$
is the state curve of the maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},z_{0})$. By (d) the
assignment is well defined: the maximal motion is unique, so $\Phi$ is a
function on $\Omega$ and not merely a relation. For fixed $t_{0}$ and $z_{0}$
the curve $t\mapsto\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0})$ is defined exactly on the maximal
interval $J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})$.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about
forces and motion, in the spacetime, frames and worldlines of
[[post-cm01-spacetime]], [[post-cm01-frames]] and [[post-cm01-worldlines]].

**(i) Setting and configuration domain.** A model of the framework has
$N\ge1$ particle labels with fixed positive masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]], clause (v)) and a configuration domain $Q$ in one
fixed inertial frame, in the unconstrained branch of
[[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a): $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open,
possibly with the collision set $\Delta$ removed when the force law of the
model is singular at coincident positions. The constrained branch of that
definition, with its reaction forces, is **not** covered by this postulate; the
dynamics of constrained systems is a separate development with its own
assumptions. A **state** of the model is a pair $z=(x,v)\in Q\times\mathbb
R^{3N}$ of positions and coordinate velocities of the labels in the chosen
frame ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]).

**(ii) Time window.** A model carries a nondegenerate open interval
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, its **time window**, read in seconds
([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(iii) Force map and standing regularity.** A **force map** on this data is a
map

$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N},\qquad (t,x,v)\longmapsto F(t,x,v)=\bigl(F_{1}(t,x,v),\dots,F_{N}(t,x,v)\bigr),$$

with components of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, read in newtons
([[def-cm01-units]]). The standing hypotheses of this branch, which every
force map of a model is required to satisfy, are:

1. **Continuity.** $F$ is continuous on its domain
   $D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
2. **State-local Lipschitz regularity, locally uniform in time.** $F$ is
   locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z=(x,v)$, locally uniformly in
   time, in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]: every
   compact cylinder $C\subseteq D$ carries a finite $L\ge0$ with
   $\lVert F(t,z)-F(t,z')\rVert_{2}\le L\lVert z-z'\rVert_{2}$ whenever
   $(t,z),(t,z')\in C$ share their time coordinate.

A map that fails clause 1 or clause 2 is **not** a force map of this branch,
whatever its other merits. When a later statement differentiates the force map
(for instance in a linearization or a smooth-dependence claim), it adds the
required differentiability hypothesis of the state variable explicitly; clause
2 alone licenses only the existence, uniqueness and continuation statements
proved on this page.

**(iv) Equation of motion.** Adopt: the motion of the labels of a model with
force map $F$ in an inertial frame is governed by

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N),$$

imposed along families of $C^{2}$ coordinate curves of the labels
$x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N}):J\to Q$, where $J\subseteq I_{0}$ is an interval with
nonempty interior and the derivatives are those of
[[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]. The precise notion of a motion of the
model, its associated first-order system and its maximal motions is
[[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. The force map is **primitive data** of the model:
the equations above are the model's law, not an operational definition of $F$
from a measured acceleration, and $F$ is not an extra observable measured
independently of the motion. The mass $m_{i}$ in (iv) is the fixed inertial
mass of clause (v) of [[post-cm01-worldlines]]; no other mass occurs in this
clause.

**(v) Additive composition of force contributions.** When a model presents its
force map as composed of contributions, the composition is the pointwise sum:
for force maps $F^{(1)},\dots,F^{(k)}$ on a common domain satisfying (iii),

$$F(t,z)=\sum_{a=1}^{k}F^{(a)}(t,z),$$

and the sum again satisfies (iii), because a finite sum of continuous maps is
continuous and a finite sum of maps that are locally Lipschitz in the state
variable is locally Lipschitz with a locally uniform constant. This
**superposition of forces** is an adopted modelling rule, not a theorem about
nature: it says how the model's total force is composed from the contributions
it declares. Two decompositions with the same sum define the same force map
and the same model; the framework does not measure an individual contribution
in isolation, and no observation of motions alone determines a decomposition.
Nor does (v) assert that sums of motions are motions: if $F$ is not affine in
the state, the sum of two solutions of (iv) generally does not satisfy (iv),
and superposing solutions is a separate question from superposing forces.

**(vi) Description in another inertial frame.** Let $F_{*}=\bigl(o',u',
(e_{1}',e_{2}',e_{3}')\bigr)$ be a second inertial frame related to the frame
of (i) by the Galilean transformation

$$t'=t+b,\qquad x'=Rx+vt+a_{0}$$

with $b\in\mathbb R$, $a_{0},v\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and $R\in SO(3)$
([[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]] clause 1;
[[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]). If $x:J\to Q$ is a family of motions of
the labels in the first frame and $\eta(t'):=R\,x(t'-b)+v\,(t'-b)+a_{0}$ is
the description of the same worldlines in the second frame, then by clause 2
of that theorem $\eta$ is of class $C^{2}$ on $J+b$ and
$\eta_{i}''(t')=R\,\ddot x_{i}(t'-b)$, so along the motion (iv) becomes

$$m_{i}\,\eta_{i}''(t')=\bigl(R\,F\bigl(t'-b,\ x(t'-b),\ \dot x(t'-b)\bigr)\bigr)_{i}.$$

Adopt: the same interaction, read in the second frame, is represented on the
transferred data by the map

$$F_{*}(t',y,w):=R\,F\Bigl(t'-b,\ R^{\mathsf T}\bigl(y-v(t'-b)-a_{0}\bigr),\ R^{\mathsf T}(w-v)\Bigr),$$

whose domain is the image of $D$ under the affine bijection
$(t',y,w)\mapsto\bigl(t'-b,\,R^{\mathsf T}(y-v(t'-b)-a_{0}),\,R^{\mathsf T}(w-v)\bigr)$;
that domain is open, and $F_{*}$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz in its
state variable because $F$ is and the transfer is an affine bijection with
bounded inverse on compacta. The framework formulates the equation of motion
in every inertial frame; a rule that does not transform by this law is a
description tied to the frame in which it was written, and the framework
attaches no kinematic covariance to it. When $Q=\mathbb R^{3N}$ — the case of
the models of the companion page — the transferred domain is again a product
$I_{0}'\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with $I_{0}'=I_{0}+b$, and
$F_{*}$ is a force map in the sense of (iii); for a bounded $Q$ the
transferred admissible position set may depend on $t'$, and the equation is
then read on that transferred set.

**(vii) What this branch excludes.** Impulsive forcing (a finite momentum
transfer at an instant is not a force map); Coulomb sliding friction, whose
expression contains the factor $v/\lvert v\rvert$ and is undefined at $v=0$;
static friction, which requires an inequality or a set-valued reaction model;
stochastic forcing; and forces that exist only as distributions. Each of these
requires its own stated model and solution notion, and none is covered by
(iii)–(iv). A singular force law is admissible on a configuration domain with
the singular configurations removed — for instance an inverse-square law on
the collision-excluded $Q$ of clause (i) — and what the removal of those
configurations implies for existence in time is stated by the continuation
theorem of this page.

**(viii) Status.** Clause (iii) states the hypotheses under which the theorems
of this page are proved; clause (iv) is the adopted law of motion; clauses (v)
and (vi) are the adopted composition and frame rules. Nothing here is deduced
from experiment, from a symmetry principle or from the uniqueness theory of
differential equations, and nothing here asserts that any physical
interaction is exactly of this form: the theorems of this page are conditional
consequences of the adopted model. The empirical significance of a concrete
model lies in fully specified model parameters and reported observations
compared with its predictions, and this postulate supplies neither.

Fix an operational observable model of the force branch
([[def-cm18-observable-model]]) in a fixed inertial frame, with parameter set
$\Theta$, preparation settings $Z$, prediction map $\Phi:\Theta\times Z\to
\mathbb R$, probability space $(\Omega,\mathfrak F,\mathbb P)$, error domain
$V\subseteq\mathbb R$ and error random element $\varepsilon$; the readout is
scalar here ($d=1$), since the mathematical sampling interface used below is
stated for real random variables, and vector readouts are treated
coordinatewise where needed.

A **repeated-observation protocol** for this model consists of

1. a **repetition count** $n\ge1$ and one error random element
   $\varepsilon_{k}:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ for each $k=1,\dots,n$, with
   $\varepsilon_{k}(\omega)\in V$ for every $\omega$, the error of the $k$-th
   repetition on the common probability space
   ([[def-probability-measure]],
   [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]]);
2. the **observations** $Y_{k}:=\Phi(\theta,z)+\varepsilon_{k}$ at a fixed
   pair $(\theta,z)\in\Theta\times Z$: the same parameter value and the same
   preparation are declared for every repetition, so that the repetition
   changes only the error.

The protocol **satisfies the IID sampling hypothesis** when the family
$(\varepsilon_{1},\dots,\varepsilon_{n})$ — equivalently the family
$(Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n})$ — is independent and identically distributed in the
sense of [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]; it
**satisfies the second-moment hypothesis** when $E\bigl[Y_{1}^{2}\bigr]<+\infty$.
Under both hypotheses the common mean and variance
$$\mu:=E[Y_{1}]\in\mathbb R,\qquad\sigma^{2}:=\operatorname{Var}(Y_{1})\in[0,+\infty)$$
are defined by [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]], the **sample mean** is
$$\overline Y:=\frac1n\sum_{k=1}^{n}Y_{k},$$
and the mathematical consequences of the two hypotheses are those of the
sampling model [[def-cm-iid-sampling-model]], namely the conclusions of
[[cor-iid-finite-variance-weak-law]]: $E\bigl\lvert\overline Y-\mu\bigr\rvert^{2}
=\sigma^{2}/n$ and, for every $a>0$,
$$\mathbb P\bigl(\bigl\lvert\overline Y-\mu\bigr\rvert\ge a\bigr) \le\frac{\sigma^{2}}{n\,a^{2}}.$$

### Well-definedness and conventions

The IID and second-moment hypotheses are **adopted model hypotheses about the
repetitions**, not consequences of the protocol and not properties of the
data. Independence of the errors fails when successive repetitions share a
systematic effect, when the apparatus drifts between repetitions or when the
same recorded data are reused; identical distribution fails when the
preparation or the conditions change between repetitions. A use of the
displayed bounds must state both hypotheses, the declared law (if any) of
$\varepsilon$, and the conditions under which the repetitions are claimed to
be comparable.

The sample mean $\overline Y$ is a random variable of the model. The
definition attaches no observed value to $\mu$ or $\sigma^{2}$; in
particular $\sigma^{2}$ is model data and not a measured uncertainty, as
[[rem-cm-inference-and-uncertainty-scope]] records for the mathematical
interface. A physical claim that a stated procedure satisfies the IID
sampling hypothesis requires separate empirical evidence and is not part of
this item.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be IID square-integrable real random variables, with $\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ and $\sigma^2=\operatorname{Var}(X_1)$. For $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^nX_k$,
$$\mathbb E|S_n/n-\mu|^2=\sigma^2/n,$$
and $S_n/n\to\mu$ in $L^2$ and in probability. Also $\mathbb P(|S_n/n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)$ for $\varepsilon>0$.

Let $X,Y$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space.
Then
$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2,$$
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y].$$
Moreover, covariance is symmetric and bilinear on finite linear combinations.
On finite full-power-set probability spaces these formulas reduce to the
published finite identities.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

derivations.claim: For every $t\in\mathbb R$ one has $x_{v}(t)=(vt,0,0)$, $w_{v}(t)=x_{v}'(t)=(v,0,0)$ and $\ddot x_{v}(t)=(0,0,0)$, so the equation $m\ddot x_{v}(t)=F(t,x_{v}(t),w_{v}(t))=0$ holds identically by [L1], and $x_{v}(0)=(0,0,0)$ with $w_{v}(0)=(v,0,0)$ matching the datum $\zeta(v)$; hence $x_{v}$ is a motion with datum $\zeta(v)$.

Adopt the spacetime assumptions of [[post-cm01-spacetime]], the frame
assumptions of [[post-cm01-frames]] and the worldline assumptions of
[[post-cm01-worldlines]]. Let

$$F=\bigl(o,u,(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})\bigr),\qquad F'=\bigl(o',u',(e_{1}',e_{2}',e_{3}')\bigr)$$

be two inertial frames of the model with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ and
$(t',x')$, and let $\gamma:I\to A$ be a worldline of a particle label described
in $F$, with coordinate curve $x:I\to\mathbb R^{3}$ and coordinate velocity and
acceleration $w=x'$ and $a=x''$ in the sense of
[[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]. Then:

1. There are $b\in\mathbb R$, $a_{0},v\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and $R\in SO(3)$
   ([[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]) such that for every event $p\in A$

$$t'(p)=t(p)+b,\qquad x'(p)=R\,x(p)+v\,t(p)+a_{0}.$$

   The parameters have dimensions $[b]=\tau$, $[a_{0,j}]=\ell$ and
   $[v_{j}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$, and $R$ is dimensionless
   ([[def-cm01-units]]); they are the ones that occur in the adopted class of
   frame changes of [[post-cm01-frames]].

2. Let $\eta:I+b\to\mathbb R^{3}$ be the coordinate curve of the same label in
   $F'$, defined by $\eta(t'):=x'(\gamma(t'-b))$ for $t'\in I+b$. Then $\eta$
   is of class $C^{2}$ and

$$\eta'(t')=R\,w(t'-b)+v,\qquad \eta''(t')=R\,a(t'-b)\qquad(t'\in I+b).$$

3. The coordinate acceleration vanishes identically in one frame exactly when
   it does in the other:

$$a\equiv0\ \text{on}\ I\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \eta''\equiv0\ \text{on}\ I+b.$$

   Equivalently, the property "the coordinate curve is an affine function of
   the frame time" is an inertial-frame-independent property of the motion.

4. Write $G(b,a_{0},v,R)$ for the transformation
   $(t,x)\mapsto(t+b,\,Rx+v\,t+a_{0})$ of the coordinate space. Then

$$G(b_{2},a_{2},v_{2},R_{2})\circ G(b_{1},a_{1},v_{1},R_{1})=G\bigl(b_{1}+b_{2},\ R_{2}a_{1}+v_{2}b_{1}+a_{2},\ R_{2}v_{1}+v_{2},\ R_{2}R_{1}\bigr)$$

and

$$G(b,a_{0},v,R)^{-1}=G\bigl(-b,\ -R^{\mathsf T}(a_{0}-vb),\ -R^{\mathsf T}v,\ R^{\mathsf T}\bigr),$$

   with all parameters again in $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3}\times\mathbb R^{3}\times SO(3)$. Consequently the Galilean transformations form a group of transformations of the coordinate space, and the relation on inertial frames "the two charts differ by a Galilean transformation" is an equivalence relation.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about frames, in the spacetime structure of [[post-cm01-spacetime]].

**(i) Rotations.** A **rotation** is a matrix $R\in SO(3)$, where

$$SO(3)=\left\{R\in\mathbb R^{3\times3}:R^{\mathsf T}R=I_{3},\ \det R=1\right\}$$

in the sense of [[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]. A rotation acts on spatial
column vectors by matrix multiplication; its entries are dimensionless under
the radian convention of [[def-cm01-units]]. Rotations are part of the
formulation of spatial changes of basis; the definition of $SO(3)$ itself
asserts nothing about physical space.

**(ii) Inertial frames.** An **inertial frame** is the global adapted affine
chart of the spacetime data determined by

$$o\in A,\qquad u\in V\ \text{with}\ \tau(u)=1,\qquad (e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})\ \text{an ordered,}\ g\text{-orthonormal, positively oriented basis of }K,$$

with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ as in [[def-cm-affine-time-space]]: the time
coordinate is $t(p)=\tau(p-o)$ and the spatial coordinates are the coefficients
of $p-o-tu\in K$ in the basis $(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3})$. Existence and uniqueness
of the coordinates, and the affine structure of the slices, are the mathematical
content of [[lem-cm-adapted-coordinates-exist-and-are-unique]] and
[[def-cm-affine-time-space]]; no physical claim beyond the reading of clause
(iii) is attached to them here.

An inertial frame is a **coordinate chart**: the triple $(o,u,(e_{i}))$. It is
definitively not an observer congruence and not a time-varying basis field. In
the model the basis $(e_{i})$ is fixed once and for all; a family of bases
depending on the time coordinate is a different structure, whose kinematics is
defined separately where it is used, and is not an inertial frame. The physical
reading of the frame is that $t$ is the model's time coordinate in seconds and
$x$ the spatial position in metres, by the conventions of
[[def-cm01-units]].

**(iii) Stationary observers.** For $x_{0}\in\mathbb R^{3}$ the curve
$\alpha_{x_{0}}:\mathbb R\to A$, $\alpha_{x_{0}}(t):=o+tu+\sum_{j=1}^{3}(x_{0})_{j}e_{j}$,
is the **observer at rest in the frame at position $x_{0}$**; the family
$\{\alpha_{x_{0}}\}_{x_{0}\in\mathbb R^{3}}$ is the **stationary observer
congruence** of the frame. Each curve has $t(\alpha_{x_{0}}(s))=s$, is
$C^{\infty}$ in adapted coordinates, and in the frame's own spatial
coordinates has constant coordinate triple $x_{0}$; each is therefore a
worldline of the model in the sense of [[post-cm01-worldlines]]. Observers of
two different inertial frames are different families of curves; the congruence
is a derived object, determined by the frame and the spacetime data, not an
additional primitive.

**(iv) Allowed changes between frames.** The model adopts the class of
transformations between inertial frames

$$t'=t+b,\qquad x'=Rx+vt+a,$$

where $b\in\mathbb R$ is a **time shift** ($[b]=\tau$), $a\in\mathbb R^{3}$ a
**spatial translation** ($[a_{i}]=\ell$), $v\in\mathbb R^{3}$ a **boost
velocity** ($[v_{i}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$) and $R\in SO(3)$ a **rotation**
($[R_{ij}]=1$). Every pair of inertial frames is related by exactly one such
transformation: that two adapted charts of the same data differ by a
transformation of this form, with $R\in SO(3)$ because both bases are
positively oriented, is the mathematical transformation law proved in
[[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]]. The kinematic
consequences of the law — the transformation of coordinate velocity and
acceleration, and the frame-independence of zero coordinate acceleration — are
proved as a statement about the model in
[[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]].

**(v) Free motion is not asserted here.** The framework's dynamics enters
through the force and equation-of-motion postulates of the pages that follow;
those pages adopt, as the content of Newton's first law, that there exist
inertial frames in the sense of clause (ii) in which a particle with zero
applied interaction has zero coordinate acceleration. This postulate
introduces the frames and their changes but asserts no dynamics: it does not
state that any particular motion has zero acceleration, and it does not
privilege any one inertial frame — each of them is a legitimate arena for the
formulation of the model's equations.

**(vi) Kinematic symmetry is not conservation.** The class (iv) is a class of
coordinate changes. Nothing in this postulate implies that any momentum,
angular momentum, energy or other quantity is conserved, or that every
mechanical system's description is invariant in form; a force law must also
transform appropriately under (iv) to be a law of the model in every frame, and
an external apparatus or background field can single out frames for the
description of a concrete experiment. Conservation statements, when they hold,
are theorems of later pages with their own hypotheses, not consequences of
this postulate.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $m,d\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, let $\mu\in U$, and let
$h:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be Borel measurable and totally differentiable at $\mu$
with total derivative $A:=Dh(\mu):\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^d$
([[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]],
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]); for instance this
holds when $h$ is $C^1$ on $U$, since continuous maps have Borel preimages of
Borel sets ([[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]]). Let
$X:\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be a random element with values in $U$,
square-integrable with mean vector $E[X]=\mu$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$
([[def-cm-covariance-matrix-of-a-random-vector]]), and define the
**linearization**
$$T:U\longrightarrow\mathbb R^d,\qquad T(x):=h(\mu)+A(x-\mu).$$
Then $T\circ X$ is a random element of $\mathbb R^d$, its mean vector is
$$E\bigl[T(X)\bigr]=h(\mu),$$
and its covariance matrix is
$$\operatorname{Cov}\bigl(T(X)\bigr)=A\Sigma A^{\mathsf T},$$
where $A$ is identified with its Jacobian matrix
$\bigl(\partial_jh_i(\mu)\bigr)_{i,j}$ and $A\Sigma A^{\mathsf T}$ is the
matrix product of [[thm-matrix-multiplication-laws]] in the matrix space of
[[def-matrix-space]].

Let $(\Omega,\mathfrak F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space
([[def-probability-measure]]), let $m\ge1$, and let
$X=(X_1,\dots,X_m):\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be a random element with target
$(\mathbb R^m,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m))$ that is **square-integrable**:
$$E\bigl[|X|^2\bigr]=\sum_{i=1}^{m}E\bigl[X_i^2\bigr]<+\infty ,$$
where $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].
Its **mean vector** is
$$\mu=E[X]:=\bigl(E[X_1],\dots,E[X_m]\bigr)\in\mathbb R^m ,$$
the coordinates being the expectations of
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]. Its **covariance matrix** is the
$m\times m$ real matrix of [[def-matrix-space]]
$$\Sigma=\operatorname{Cov}(X):=\bigl(\Sigma_{ij}\bigr)_{i,j=1}^{m},\qquad \Sigma_{ij}:=E\bigl[(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)\bigr]\in\mathbb R .$$
For a random vector $Y$ the entries $\Sigma_{ij}$ are also written
$\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$, and $\Sigma_{ii}=\operatorname{Var}(X_i)$.

### Well-definedness and elementary properties

**Integrability of the entries.** Square-integrability gives
$E[X_i^2]<+\infty$ for each $i$. Since $X$ takes values in a probability
space, the elementary inequality
$$|X_i|\le \tfrac12\bigl(1+X_i^2\bigr)$$
and monotonicity and homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]) show that each
$X_i$ is integrable, so $\mu_i=E[X_i]$ is a finite real number
([[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]]). Likewise
$$|X_i-\mu_i|\le |X_i|+|\mu_i|\le \tfrac12\bigl(1+X_i^2\bigr)+|\mu_i|,$$
so $X_i-\mu_i$ is square-integrable and integrable. Finally
$$|(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)|\le \tfrac12\bigl((X_i-\mu_i)^2+(X_j-\mu_j)^2\bigr),$$
and the right-hand side is integrable by additivity, monotonicity and
homogeneity of the nonnegative integral
([[cor-additivity-of-the-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]],
[[prop-order-and-scalar-rules-for-the-nonnegative-integral]]); hence every
$\Sigma_{ij}$ is a finite real number.

**Symmetry.** For all $i,j$ the real numbers $(X_i-\mu_i)(X_j-\mu_j)$ and
$(X_j-\mu_j)(X_i-\mu_i)$ are equal pointwise, so $\Sigma_{ij}=\Sigma_{ji}$;
thus $\Sigma^{\mathsf T}=\Sigma$.

**Positive semidefiniteness.** Let $z=(z_1,\dots,z_m)\in\mathbb R^m$. The
random variable $W:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_iX_i$ is a finite linear combination of
square-integrable random variables, hence square-integrable, and bilinearity
of covariance ([[lem-variance-and-covariance-identities-for-random-variables]])
gives
$$z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=\sum_{i,j=1}^{m}z_iz_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j) =\operatorname{Cov}(W,W)=\operatorname{Var}(W) =E\bigl[(W-E[W])^2\bigr]\ge0 ,$$
the inequality holding because $(W-E[W])^2\ge0$ pointwise and expectation is
monotone ([[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]]). In
particular $z^{\mathsf T}\Sigma z=0$ exactly when $W$ is almost surely
constant, so $\Sigma$ is positive definite exactly when for every $z\neq0$
the random variable $\sum_{i=1}^{m}z_iX_i$ fails to be almost surely
constant.

No independence hypothesis is used anywhere in this definition; $\Sigma$
records the pairwise covariances of the coordinates.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability
space.

1. For scalars $a,b$,
   $$\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\,\mathbb E[X]+b\,\mathbb E[Y].$$
2. If $X$ and $Y$ are real-valued and $X\le Y$ almost surely, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]\le\mathbb E[Y].$$
3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

In a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$, events $A\subseteq B\subseteq\Omega$ satisfy
$$0\le\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)\le1,$$
and
$$\mathbb P(\varnothing)=0,\qquad \mathbb P(\Omega)=1,\qquad \mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A),\qquad \mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A).$$
Probability zero need not imply that an event is empty.

Let $((\Omega_i,w_i))_{i\in I}$ be a finite indexed family of finite probability spaces. Their **product probability space** has outcome set
$$\Omega:=\prod_{i\in I}\Omega_i$$
and assigns $\omega=(\omega_i)_{i\in I}$ the weight
$$w(\omega):=\prod_{i\in I}w_i(\omega_i).$$
For $I=\varnothing$, the product outcome set is the singleton containing the empty function and its weight is the empty product $1$. Normalization and independence of coordinate events are proved in [[thm-product-probability-has-independent-coordinate-events]].

The weights in every finite product of finite probability spaces are nonnegative and sum to $1$. For events $A_i\subseteq\Omega_i$, the coordinate events
$$C_i:=\{\omega\in\prod_{j\in I}\Omega_j:\omega_i\in A_i\}$$
are mutually independent, and for every $J\subseteq I$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcap_{j\in J}C_j\right)=\prod_{j\in J}\mathbb P_j(A_j).$$

For $p\in[0,1]$, a **Bernoulli$(p)$ random variable** takes the value $1$ with probability $p$ and $0$ with probability $1-p$.

For $n\in\mathbb N$, a **binomial$(n,p)$ random variable** is a sum $X=\sum_{i<n}X_i$ of $n$ mutually independent Bernoulli$(p)$ variables. When $n=0$, this is the constant zero random variable.

derivations.claim: Let $p\in(0,1)$ and let $\Omega_{0}:=\{0,1\}$ with weights $w_{0}(1):=p$ and $w_{0}(0):=1-p$; these weights are nonnegative and sum to $1$, so $(\Omega_{0},w_{0})$ is a finite probability space in the sense of [L1], and the event $A_{0}:=\{1\}$ has $\mathbb P(A_{0})=p$ by [L3], with $A_{0}\neq\varnothing$ and $\mathbb P(A_{0})\in(0,1)$.

For $n\ge1$ form the finite product of $n$ copies of $(\Omega_{0},w_{0})$: the outcome set is $\Omega:=\{0,1\}^{n}$ with weights $w(\omega)=\prod_{k=1}^{n}w_{0}(\omega_{k})$, a finite probability space by [L2]; the single-observation event of the refuted statement corresponds to the coordinate event $C_{k}:=\{\omega_{k}=1\}$ in the $k$-th coordinate, with coordinate probability $p$ by mutual independence of the coordinates in [L2], and reading $Y_{k}:=\omega_{k}$ as the $k$-th observation makes the family $(Y_{k})_{k\le n}$ identically distributed by construction and mutually independent by [L2], so it satisfies the IID sampling hypothesis of [[def-cm18-sampling-model]]; each $Y_{k}$ is bounded, so the second-moment hypothesis holds as well.

The event "no outcome in $A$ occurs in the finite sample" is $E:=\{\omega\in\Omega:\omega_{k}=0\ \text{for every }k\le n\}=\bigcap_{k=1}^{n}\{\omega_{k}=0\}$; by the product formula of [L2] applied to the coordinate events $\{\omega_{k}=0\}$, whose coordinate probabilities are $1-p$, one has $\mathbb P(E)=\prod_{k=1}^{n}(1-p)=(1-p)^{n}$.
Since $0<p<1$ one has $0<1-p<1$ and therefore $0<(1-p)^{n}<1$ for every $n\ge1$; the event $E$ of a finite sample with no outcome in $A$ has strictly positive probability.

Under the product model of steps 1.2 and 2.1 the single observation lies in the designated event with probability $p\in(0,1)$, the coordinates are mutually independent, and yet the finite sample avoids the event with positive probability $(1-p)^{n}$ by step 3.1; therefore the implication asserted in the refuted statement is false: a finite sample with no outcome in $A$ can occur with positive probability under the declared sampling model, so its occurrence does not refute that model.

The probability that at least one outcome in $A$ is seen in the finite sample is $1-(1-p)^{n}$, which tends to $1$ as $n$ grows but equals $1$ for no finite $n$ when $0<p<1$; the failure to exhibit the feature in a finite sample is a positive-probability event of the model, not a refutation of it.
